* Returning an unchanged child draft, such as `draft.list`, makes its value the next state; returning a changed one throws an error.
* Mutative searches a returned object for drafts and replaces each one with its value, so a returned value can hold drafts, such as `{ ...draft, count: 0 }`. [`rawReturn()`](/docs/api-reference/rawreturn) skips that search for a value that holds no drafts, and development builds warn when a returned object holds no drafts to suggest it.

## Async recipes [#async-recipes]

The recipe can be an async function: `create()` then returns a Promise of the result, and the draft stays usable until that Promise settles.

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = { items: ['a'] };

const state = await create(baseState, async (draft) => {
  const item = await Promise.resolve('b');
  draft.items.push(item);
});

expect(state.items).toEqual(['a', 'b']);
```

`create()` recognizes the Promises of the current JavaScript realm only, so an async function from another realm, such as a `vm` context or an iframe, needs a wrapper from this realm: `create(baseState, async (draft) => { return await recipe(draft); })`. TypeScript types the result as a Promise as well, except with an explicit state type that is a type parameter, as in `create<T>(base, async (draft) => { … })` in a generic function, or that includes Promises, such as `object` or `unknown`, which gives the state type itself. In generic code, leave out the type argument: `create(base, async (draft) => { … })` gives `Promise<T>`, and `create(async (draft: T) => { … })` gives `(base: T) => Promise<T>`.

## Currying [#currying]

With a recipe and no base state, `create()` returns a producer, which takes the base state and passes its other arguments to the recipe:

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

type Todo = { text: string; done: boolean };

const toggle = create((draft: Todo[], index: number) => {
  draft[index].done = !draft[index].done;
});

const todos: Todo[] = [{ text: 'learn', done: false }];

expect(toggle(todos, 0)).toEqual([{ text: 'learn', done: true }]);
```

With a base state and no recipe, `create()` returns a draft and a `finalize()` function, which returns what `create()` returns with a recipe:

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = { list: [{ text: 'todo' }] };

const [draft, finalize] = create(baseState, { enablePatches: true });
draft.list.push({ text: 'learning' });
const [state, patches] = finalize();

expect(state.list).toHaveLength(2);
expect(patches).toEqual([
  { op: 'add', path: ['list', 1], value: { text: 'learning' } },
]);
```

<Callout type="warn">
  Call `finalize()` only once. When it throws, for example because a development build rejects a patch path, the drafts are not revoked as they are when a recipe fails: they stay writable, and a second `finalize()` returns a state that can hold a revoked draft, with patches that miss changes. Create a new draft from the base state instead.
</Callout>

See [Currying](/docs/advanced-guides/currying) for more.

## create() on a draft [#create-on-a-draft]

A recipe can pass a draft to a helper that calls `create()`. Unlike Immer's `produce`, which drafts the draft itself, `create()` drafts a copy of its current state, `current(draft)`: the values that the helper's recipe leaves unchanged are objects of the base state. Assigning the result back into the outer draft is safe, but changing one of those values afterwards changes the base state, because the outer draft returns an assigned value as it is ([#160](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/issues/160)). Development builds warn once when `create()` receives a draft with a recipe.

```ts
const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.node = create(draft.node, (node) => {
    node.name = 'renamed';
  });
  // `draft.node` is now the helper's result, and `draft.node.metadata` is an
  // object of `baseState`: writing to it here would change `baseState`.
});
```

To avoid it, let such a helper change a draft in place, and call `create()` only on other values:

```ts
type Item = { name: string; metadata: { value: string } };

function rename(item: Item, name: string): Item {
  if (isDraft(item)) {
    item.name = name;
    return item;
  }
  return create(item, (draft) => {
    draft.name = name;
  });
}
```

On a draft, `rename()` returns the draft itself, so the outer recipe changes its result through the outer draft, and the values that it leaves unchanged keep their references. Unlike a call to `create()`, it changes the outer draft even if the caller discards the result.

Where that does not fit, make such changes in the helper's recipe, or through the outer draft before calling the helper. If the helper's result must not share objects with the base state, give `create()` a deep copy, as in `create(structuredClone(current(draft)), recipe)`, at the cost of copying the draft on each call and of new references for the values that the recipe leaves unchanged; `structuredClone` turns class instances into plain objects and throws on functions. To catch such writes, enable `enableAutoFreeze` in development, for example with `makeCreator({ enableAutoFreeze: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production' })` for such helpers: it freezes the helper's result together with the objects of the base state that it shares, so a write to them throws instead of changing the base state, as Immer's default auto-freeze does.

A draft belongs to the `create()` call that made it, also the draft that `create(base)` returns. Do not store it in the draft of another call, or in an object that you assign there: it is revoked when its own call ends, so the other call's result can hold a draft that throws when it is read, and a Set draft that received it may no longer find it with `has()` or `delete()`. Store `current(draft)`, the original object or the result of that call instead.

## Errors [#errors]

The errors that `create()` throws, such as for an invalid base state or for a recipe that changes the draft and returns another value, are listed with their production codes on the [errors page](/docs/extra-topics/errors).


# current() (/docs/api-reference/current)

Take a snapshot of the current value of a draft, as plain objects without proxies.

`current(draft)` returns a snapshot of the current value of a draft: plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets with the changes that the recipe has made so far, without the proxies of the draft. The snapshot stays valid after the recipe ends, so it can be logged, compared, kept or searched.

```ts
current<T>(draft: Draft<T>): T
```

## Usage [#usage]

```ts
import { create, current } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  foo: 'bar',
  list: [{ text: 'todo' }],
};

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.foo = 'foobar';
  draft.list.push({ text: 'learning' });

  const snapshot = current(draft.list);
  expect(snapshot).toEqual([{ text: 'todo' }, { text: 'learning' }]);

  draft.list.push({ text: 'shipping' });
  // Later changes do not reach the snapshot.
  expect(snapshot).toHaveLength(2);
});
```

* The snapshot shares every object that the recipe has not changed with the base state. For a draft that the recipe has not changed, `current(draft)` returns its original value, which [`original(draft)`](/docs/api-reference/original) also returns, without copying it.
* A changed draft is copied, together with its changed descendants, on every call, so each call returns new objects for it. Take one snapshot for a series of reads rather than calling `current()` in a loop.
* Later changes to the draft do not change the snapshot, except changes to objects that are not drafted, such as class instances that no mark makes draftable, which the snapshot shares with the draft.
* `current()` does not freeze the snapshot, also with `enableAutoFreeze`.
* `current()` throws for a value that is not a draft, such as the base state or a finished state; use [`isDraft()`](/docs/api-reference/isdraft) to check.

## Searching a large array [#searching-a-large-array]

Every object read through a draft becomes a draft of its own, so `draft.list.find()` pays for a draft per visited element. Searching `current(draft.list)` reads plain values instead: the original array while the recipe has not changed it, and otherwise a copy that holds the current value of each changed element and the original object of every other one. Its indices are those of the draft, also after the recipe added, removed or moved elements. Change the match through the draft. Its elements are not drafts, so the callback must only read them.

```ts
import { create, current } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  list: Array.from({ length: 1000 }, (_, id) => ({ id, done: false })),
};

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.list.shift();
  const index = current(draft.list).findIndex((item) => item.id === 500);
  draft.list[index].done = true;
});

expect(state.list[499]).toEqual({ id: 500, done: true });
expect(state.list[0]).toBe(baseState.list[1]);
```

In [strict mode](/docs/advanced-guides/strict-mode), development builds warn once when a recipe leaves 1,000 or more drafts unchanged, which is what a search through a large draft array does.

<Callout type="idea">
  [`original(draft.list)`](/docs/api-reference/original) searches the base state instead, whose indices no longer match those of the draft once the recipe has added, removed or moved elements.
</Callout>

The functions that Mutative exports, with their options, results and errors.

- [apply()](/docs/api-reference/apply)
- [makeCreator()](/docs/api-reference/makecreator)
- [current()](/docs/api-reference/current)
- [original()](/docs/api-reference/original)
- [rawReturn()](/docs/api-reference/rawreturn)
- [unsafe()](/docs/api-reference/unsafe)
- [isDraftable()](/docs/api-reference/isdraftable)
- [isDraft()](/docs/api-reference/isdraft)
- [markSimpleObject()](/docs/api-reference/marksimpleobject)
- [Type casts](/docs/api-reference/casts)


# isDraft() (/docs/api-reference/isdraft)

Check whether a value is a draft.

`isDraft(value)` returns `true` for a draft, of the current recipe or of any other one, and `false` for any other value, including the base state, a finished state and the values that a recipe assigned.

```ts
isDraft(value: any): boolean
```

## Usage [#usage]

```ts
import { create, isDraft } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  date: new Date(),
  list: [{ text: 'todo' }],
};

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  expect(isDraft(draft)).toBe(true);
  expect(isDraft(draft.list)).toBe(true);
  // A Date is not drafted.
  expect(isDraft(draft.date)).toBe(false);
});

expect(isDraft(state)).toBe(false);
expect(isDraft(baseState)).toBe(false);
```

Use it in helpers that take a draft or a plain value, for example to change a draft in place and to call `create()` for any other value, as [`create()` on a draft](/docs/api-reference/create#create-on-a-draft) shows. [`current()`](/docs/api-reference/current) and [`original()`](/docs/api-reference/original) throw for values that are not drafts.

`isDraft()` reads the value, so for a draft whose producer has ended, which Mutative revokes, it throws as any other read does.


# isDraftable() (/docs/api-reference/isdraftable)

Check whether Mutative drafts a value, optionally with a mark.

`isDraftable(value, options?)` returns `true` for a value that Mutative can draft, and which `create()` therefore accepts as its base state.

```ts
isDraftable(value: any, options?: { mark?: Mark }): boolean
```

## Usage [#usage]

```ts
import { isDraftable } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  date: new Date(),
  list: [{ text: 'todo' }],
};

expect(isDraftable(baseState)).toBe(true);
expect(isDraftable(baseState.list)).toBe(true);
expect(isDraftable(baseState.date)).toBe(false);
```

Without a mark, these values are draftable:

* Plain objects, whose prototype is `Object.prototype`.
* Arrays.
* `Map` and `Set` instances, also of their subclasses.

Other values are not: primitives, functions, dates, class instances, objects without a prototype, and plain objects of other realms, such as iframes. A [mark](/docs/advanced-guides/mark) makes them draftable, as [`markSimpleObject()`](/docs/api-reference/marksimpleobject) does for objects without a prototype and plain objects of other realms. Pass the same `mark` that the `create()` calls use, to get their answer:

```ts
import { isDraftable } from 'mutative';

class Todo {
  constructor(public text: string) {}
}

const mark = (target: unknown) =>
  target instanceof Todo ? ('immutable' as const) : undefined;

expect(isDraftable(new Todo('learn'))).toBe(false);
expect(isDraftable(new Todo('learn'), { mark })).toBe(true);
```

A mark makes a value draftable when it returns `'immutable'` or a function that copies the value. A mark that returns `'mutable'` keeps a value out of drafts when a recipe reads it, but `isDraftable()` still returns `true` for plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets.


# makeCreator() (/docs/api-reference/makecreator)

Make a create() function with default options.

`makeCreator(options)` returns a `create()` function whose [options](/docs/api-reference/create#options) default to the given ones. Use it to set options once for an application, a store or a module, instead of passing them to each call.

```ts
makeCreator(options?: Options): typeof create
```

## Usage [#usage]

```ts
import { makeCreator } from 'mutative';

const create = makeCreator({
  enablePatches: true,
});

const baseState = {
  foo: {
    bar: 'str',
  },
};

const [state, patches, inversePatches] = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.foo.bar = 'new str';
});

expect(state).toEqual({ foo: { bar: 'new str' } });
expect(patches).toEqual([
  { op: 'replace', path: ['foo', 'bar'], value: 'new str' },
]);
expect(inversePatches).toEqual([
  { op: 'replace', path: ['foo', 'bar'], value: 'str' },
]);
```

The returned function has every signature of [`create()`](/docs/api-reference/create): it takes a base state and a recipe, a recipe alone for a [curried producer](/docs/advanced-guides/currying), or a base state alone for a manual draft.

## Overriding the defaults [#overriding-the-defaults]

The options of a call override the defaults of the creator, option by option:

```ts
import { makeCreator } from 'mutative';

const create = makeCreator({
  enablePatches: true,
});

const baseState = { count: 0 };

// The defaults: patches on.
const [state, patches] = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.count += 1;
});

// Patches off for this call only.
const nextState = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    draft.count += 1;
  },
  {
    enablePatches: false,
  }
);

expect(patches).toHaveLength(1);
expect(nextState).toEqual(state);
```

TypeScript types the result of each call from the options that apply to it, so the call with `enablePatches: false` returns the state alone.

## Examples [#examples]

Checks for development builds only, such as strict mode and auto-freeze:

```ts
import { makeCreator } from 'mutative';

const isDevelopment = process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production';

export const create = makeCreator({
  strict: isDevelopment,
  enableAutoFreeze: isDevelopment,
});
```

The same `mark` for every call on state that holds class instances:

```ts
import { makeCreator } from 'mutative';

class Point {
  constructor(
    public x: number,
    public y: number
  ) {}
}

const create = makeCreator({
  mark: (target, { immutable }) =>
    target instanceof Point ? immutable : undefined,
});

const baseState = { points: [new Point(0, 0)] };

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.points[0].x = 1;
});

expect(state.points[0]).toBeInstanceOf(Point);
expect(state.points[0].x).toBe(1);
expect(baseState.points[0].x).toBe(0);
```

Pass the same `mark` to [`apply()`](/docs/api-reference/apply) and [`isDraftable()`](/docs/api-reference/isdraftable) for that state.

<Callout type="idea">
  Each creator keeps its own options, unlike Immer's global settings, so libraries and applications that use Mutative do not change each other's behavior.
</Callout>


# markSimpleObject() (/docs/api-reference/marksimpleobject)

A mark that drafts objects without a prototype and plain objects of other realms.

`markSimpleObject` is a [mark](/docs/advanced-guides/mark) that makes simple objects draftable: plain objects, objects without a prototype, such as those of `Object.create(null)`, and plain objects of other realms, such as same-origin iframes or `vm` contexts, whose prototype is that realm's `Object.prototype`. Without it, Mutative drafts only plain objects of its own realm, and `create()` throws for a base state of the other kinds.

```ts
markSimpleObject(value: unknown): 'immutable' | undefined
```

## Usage [#usage]

Pass it as the `mark` option, of a call or of [`makeCreator()`](/docs/api-reference/makecreator):

```ts
import { create, markSimpleObject } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  foo: {
    bar: 'str',
  },
  simpleObject: Object.create(null),
};

const state = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    draft.foo.bar = 'new str';
    draft.simpleObject.a = 'a';
  },
  {
    mark: markSimpleObject,
  }
);

expect(state.simpleObject).not.toBe(baseState.simpleObject);
expect(state.simpleObject.a).toBe('a');
expect(Object.getPrototypeOf(state.simpleObject)).toBe(null);
expect(baseState.simpleObject.a).toBe(undefined);
```

It returns `'immutable'` for simple objects and nothing for other values, which Mutative then drafts as usual, so it combines with other marks in an array, as in `mark: [markSimpleObject, markClasses]`. Like any immutable mark, it works with patches and auto-freeze.


# original() (/docs/api-reference/original)

Get the value that a draft was created from, without the changes of the recipe.

`original(draft)` returns the value that a draft was created from: the object of the base state, without the changes that the recipe has made to it.

```ts
original<T>(draft: T): T
```

## Usage [#usage]

```ts
import { create, original } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  foo: 'bar',
  list: [{ text: 'todo' }],
};

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.foo = 'foobar';
  draft.list.push({ text: 'learning' });

  expect(original(draft.list)).toEqual([{ text: 'todo' }]);
  expect(original(draft.list)).toBe(baseState.list);
  expect(original(draft.list)).not.toBe(draft.list);
});
```

Use it to compare a draft with its original value, or to read the base state without creating drafts, since the original value holds no proxies.

* `original()` returns the object of the base state itself, so never change it.
* It throws for a value that is not a draft, such as the base state, a finished state, or a value that the recipe assigned, which Mutative does not draft. Use [`isDraft()`](/docs/api-reference/isdraft) to check.
* An object of the base state is drafted when the recipe reads it, so a search of a draft array for such an object does not find it; search `original(draft.list)` for it, as in `original(draft.list).indexOf(item)`.

`original()` reflects the state before the recipe's changes, so an index found in `original(draft.list)` no longer matches the draft once the recipe has added, removed or moved elements. To search a draft array, use [`current()`](/docs/api-reference/current#searching-a-large-array).


# rawReturn() (/docs/api-reference/rawreturn)

Return a value from a recipe as it is, without searching it for drafts, or return undefined.

`rawReturn(value)` wraps the value that a recipe returns, so that `create()` makes it the next state as it is, without searching it for drafts. It also makes `undefined` the next state, which a recipe that returns nothing cannot.

```ts
rawReturn<T extends object | undefined>(value: T): T
```

## Usage [#usage]

```ts
import { create, rawReturn } from 'mutative';

const baseState = { id: 'test' };

const state = create(baseState as { id: string } | undefined, () => {
  return rawReturn(undefined);
});

expect(state).toBe(undefined);
```

A recipe can return a new state instead of changing the draft. Mutative searches such a value for drafts and replaces each one with its value, so that a returned value can hold drafts, as `{ ...draft, a: 2 }` does:

```ts
import { create, isDraft } from 'mutative';

const baseState = { a: 1, b: { c: 1 } };

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  return {
    ...draft,
    a: 2,
  };
});

expect(state).toEqual({ a: 2, b: { c: 1 } });
expect(isDraft(state.b)).toBe(false);
expect(state.b).toBe(baseState.b);
```

That search visits every object of the returned value, which takes time for large values. `rawReturn()` skips it for a value that holds no drafts, such as a state built from scratch or an earlier state:

```ts
import { create, rawReturn } from 'mutative';

const initialState = { todos: [] as string[] };
const baseState = { todos: ['learn'] };

// A reducer that resets the state.
const state = create(baseState, () => rawReturn(initialState));

expect(state).toBe(initialState);
```

In the benchmark, returning a new state of 10,000 rows took 2.6 ms with the search and 0.26 µs with `rawReturn()`. Development builds warn when a returned object holds no drafts, to suggest `rawReturn()`.

## Performance compared with Immer [#performance-compared-with-immer]

Returning an earlier state is the one workload of the [benchmark](/docs/getting-started/performance) in which Mutative's defaults were slower than Immer's. Immer freezes each next state by default and skips frozen values when it searches a returned state for drafts, so returning a state that it had frozen earlier took it 0.79 µs at 10,000 rows, while Mutative, which does not freeze by default, searched the same state for 2.6 ms. With the same settings, Mutative was faster: 2.6 ms against 5.7 ms without auto-freeze, and 0.53 µs against 0.79 µs with it, since its production builds skip frozen values too. `rawReturn()` returns a state that holds no drafts in 0.26 µs.

Freezing by default is a trade-off rather than a shortcut. Data that is not frozen yet, such as a response parsed from JSON, has to be frozen first: returning 10,000 rows that each call creates took Immer 9.2 ms with its default, against 3.1 ms for Mutative's search and 0.23 ms with `rawReturn()`, of which creating the rows took 0.19 ms. Freezing also made Immer slower in every other workload of the [selected results](/docs/getting-started/performance#mutative-vs-immer), such as 25.0 µs instead of 1.82 µs to update an item of 100 rows. [Auto Freeze](/docs/advanced-guides/auto-freeze) describes when freezing is worth its cost.

## Rules [#rules]

* Never wrap a value that holds drafts. Without strict mode, Mutative does not search it, so the next state keeps those drafts, which are revoked when the recipe ends and throw when they are read. In [strict mode](/docs/advanced-guides/strict-mode), Mutative still searches a value that `rawReturn()` wraps and replaces its drafts, and development builds warn: `The return value contains drafts, please don't use 'rawReturn()' to wrap the return value.`
* Call it with exactly one argument; it throws otherwise.
* Wrap only objects and `undefined`. A recipe can return a primitive as it is, since a primitive holds no drafts, and development builds warn when `rawReturn()` receives one.
* With auto-freeze, production builds do not search frozen objects in a returned value or the values they hold, so returning an earlier, frozen state, or state built from one, costs little even without `rawReturn()`. Development builds still search them and throw when they find a draft there, so never put a draft in a frozen object or in a value it holds.

<Callout type="idea">
  Enable strict mode in development when you use `rawReturn()`, for example with `strict: process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'`, so that a wrapped value that holds drafts is reported.
</Callout>


# unsafe() (/docs/api-reference/unsafe)

Read values that are not drafted in strict mode.

In [strict mode](/docs/advanced-guides/strict-mode), reading an object that Mutative does not draft throws, such as a `Date`, a class instance that no mark makes draftable, or a value that a `mark` makes mutable. `unsafe(callback)` runs the callback with such reads allowed and returns what it returns.

```ts
unsafe<T>(callback: () => T): T
```

## Usage [#usage]

```ts
import { create, unsafe } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  createdAt: new Date(Date.UTC(2020, 0, 1)),
  updatedAt: new Date(Date.UTC(2020, 0, 1)),
};

const state = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    // Reading a Date from a draft throws in strict mode:
    expect(() => draft.createdAt.getTime()).toThrow();

    const year = unsafe(() => draft.createdAt.getUTCFullYear());
    expect(year).toBe(2020);

    // Assigning a value is no read and needs no unsafe().
    draft.updatedAt = new Date(Date.UTC(2021, 0, 1));
  },
  {
    strict: true,
  }
);

expect(state.updatedAt.getUTCFullYear()).toBe(2021);
expect(baseState.updatedAt.getUTCFullYear()).toBe(2020);
```

Strict mode makes such reads explicit because Mutative does not copy the values that it does not draft: the draft and the base state share them, so a change to one of them, such as `draft.createdAt.setFullYear(2000)`, changes the base state as well, and the next state holds the same object. Replace such values, as the recipe above replaces `updatedAt`, or [mark](/docs/advanced-guides/mark) their class as `immutable` so that Mutative drafts and copies them.

* `unsafe()` allows the reads of all producers until its callback returns. A nested call keeps the access of the outer call until the outer one returns.
* Outside strict mode, `unsafe()` only calls the callback.
* Values that a recipe reads inside `unsafe()` are still drafts when they are draftable, so changes to them are recorded as usual.


# Comparison with Immer (/docs/extra-topics/comparison-with-immer)

Every difference between Mutative and Immer 11.1.18 in APIs, defaults, drafts and patches, and the behaviors that both share.

Mutative and Immer work the same way: a recipe changes a draft, and the library produces the next state, which shares every part that the recipe left unchanged. Most code moves from Immer by renaming its functions, as the [migration guide](/docs/advanced-guides/migration) shows. This page lists the differences that change what code does or produces, checked against Immer 11.1.18, and the behaviors that both libraries share where it is easy to assume otherwise.

## At a glance [#at-a-glance]

|                                                      | Mutative |     Immer     |
| :--------------------------------------------------- | :------: | :-----------: |
| Auto-freeze off by default                           |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| Options per call, without global settings or plugins |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| Drafts of class instances without changing the class |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| Custom shallow copies                                |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| Strict mode                                          |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| Async recipes                                        |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| Map and Set subclasses keep their class              |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| ES2025 Set methods on Set drafts                     |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| Freezing reaches the objects used as Map keys        |     ✅    |       ❌       |
| Array methods that run natively on drafts            |     ✅    | Opt-in plugin |
| JSON Pointer string paths in patches                 |     ✅    |       ❌       |

## APIs [#apis]

| Immer                                                             | Mutative                                                                                          |
| :---------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `produce(base, recipe)`                                           | `create(base, recipe)`                                                                            |
| `produce(recipe)`, a curried producer                             | `create(recipe)`                                                                                  |
| `produceWithPatches()`, or a patch listener passed to `produce()` | `create(base, recipe, { enablePatches: true })`, which returns `[state, patches, inversePatches]` |
| `applyPatches(state, patches)`                                    | `apply(state, patches)`                                                                           |
| `createDraft(base)` and `finishDraft(draft)`                      | `const [draft, finalize] = create(base)` and `finalize()`                                         |
| `current()`, `original()`, `isDraft()`, `isDraftable()`           | The same functions; `isDraftable()` also takes `{ mark }`                                         |
| `castDraft()`, `castImmutable()`                                  | The same functions, and `castMutable()`                                                           |
| `nothing`, to return `undefined`                                  | `rawReturn(undefined)`                                                                            |
| `[immerable]: true` on a class                                    | The `mark` option, or `markSimpleObject()`                                                        |
| `freeze(value, deep)`                                             | No export; `enableAutoFreeze` freezes results                                                     |
| `setAutoFreeze()`                                                 | The `enableAutoFreeze` option of each call                                                        |
| `new Immer(config)`                                               | `makeCreator(options)`, which returns a `create()` with these options                             |
| `enableMapSet()`, `enablePatches()`                               | Not needed                                                                                        |
| `enableArrayMethods()`                                            | Not needed; array methods run natively                                                            |
| `setUseStrictShallowCopy()`, `setUseStrictIteration()`            | No settings; see [Marking](#defaults-and-configuration)                                           |
| No counterpart                                                    | `unsafe()`, for reads in strict mode                                                              |

## Defaults and configuration [#defaults-and-configuration]

* **Auto-freeze.** Mutative leaves results unfrozen unless `enableAutoFreeze` is set, while Immer freezes them by default. With freezing on, both freeze the whole result deeply, unchanged parts included, and freeze Map and Set instances so that their mutators throw. Mutative also freezes the objects that a Map uses as keys, which Immer leaves unfrozen.
* **Options per call.** Each `create()` and `apply()` call takes its own options, and `makeCreator()` sets defaults, where Immer's `setAutoFreeze()` and its plugins change the module for every caller. Maps, Sets and patches work without the `enableMapSet()` and `enablePatches()` calls that Immer requires and throws without.
* **Marking.** A `mark` function decides how values are drafted: it can make class instances draftable without changing their class, where Immer requires an `[immerable]` property on it, keep values mutable so that the recipe changes them in place, or return a function that copies a value. Mutative copies a class instance that a mark makes draftable with all its own properties, non-enumerable ones included, as Immer does with `setUseStrictShallowCopy('class_only')`, but assigns those that are enumerable, writable and configurable, as Immer's default copy does, so an own property that shadows a setter of the class runs it; see [Copying marked instances](/docs/advanced-guides/mark#copying-marked-instances). Both copy only the enumerable properties of plain objects and read their getters as values. See [mark](/docs/advanced-guides/mark).
* **Strict mode.** With `strict: true`, reading a value that the recipe could change without a draft, such as a class instance that is not marked, throws unless the read happens inside `unsafe()`. Immer has no such mode. See [strict mode](/docs/advanced-guides/strict-mode).

## Drafts [#drafts]

* **Map and Set subclasses** keep their class and its methods, in drafts and in the next state. Immer's next state holds plain Maps and Sets instead.
* **ES2025 Set methods**, such as `union()` and `isSubsetOf()`, work on Set drafts and compare objects as iterating the draft returns them; see the [FAQ](/docs/extra-topics/faq#do-the-set-methods-such-as-union-and-issubsetof-work-on-set-drafts). On Immer's Set drafts they do not see the draft's items: `union()` of a draft of `new Set([1, 2])` with `new Set([3])` returns `Set {3}`.
* **Async recipes** make `create()` return a Promise of the result, and the draft stays usable until the Promise settles; see [create()](/docs/api-reference/create). Immer 11 throws, because the returned Promise counts as a new value while the recipe changed the draft.
* **A draft passed to a nested `create()`** is copied, where Immer's `produce()` drafts the draft itself; see [create() on a draft](/docs/api-reference/create#create-on-a-draft).
* **Returned values.** Both replace the state with a value that the recipe returns, and both throw when the recipe also changed the draft. `rawReturn()` returns `undefined`, as Immer's `nothing` does, and also returns a value without searching it for drafts; see [rawReturn()](/docs/api-reference/rawreturn).
* **Array methods.** `shift()`, `unshift()`, `splice()` and `reverse()` move the elements of a plain array on its copy, and `indexOf()`, `lastIndexOf()` and `includes()` search it natively, under the contract that the [FAQ](/docs/extra-topics/faq#which-array-methods-run-natively-on-drafts) describes. Immer runs them through the proxy unless its opt-in `enableArrayMethods()` plugin is enabled, which in Immer 11.1.18 can return raw base objects and emit patches that fail to replay; see the [audit](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/test/immer-array-methods.md).
* **Alike in both.** Each path to a shared object gets its own draft; see [shared references](/docs/extra-topics/shared-references). A class instance that is neither marked nor `[immerable]` is not drafted, so a recipe that changes it changes the base state. `current()` and `original()` throw for values that are not drafts. An iteration over a Map draft that starts before the recipe changes the Map walks the base Map, in both libraries; see the [FAQ](/docs/extra-topics/faq#can-a-recipe-change-a-map-draft-while-iterating-over-it).

## Patches [#patches]

Both libraries emit the same patches for most changes: the same operations, paths and values, the patches of nested drafts before those of their parents, and values that are the objects of the next state, frozen with it when freezing is on. They differ in the following cases; [Patches](/docs/advanced-guides/patches#patch-behavior) describes how Mutative generates and applies them.

* **Arrays that get shorter.** By default, Mutative records a shorter array with a `replace` patch of its `length`, as in the patches of `pop()` and `list.length = 0` and in the inverse patches of `push()` and of a `splice()` that inserts, while Immer removes each index with a `remove` patch. With `enablePatches: { arrayLengthAssignment: false }`, Mutative emits the same `remove` patches as Immer.
* **Changed items of a Set.** When a recipe changes objects in a Set without adding or removing items, Mutative emits a `replace` patch under the position of each changed item, while Immer removes the old object and adds the new one. Once the recipe adds or removes items, both carry the changed items by value.
* **String paths.** With `enablePatches: { pathAsArray: false }`, Mutative emits paths as JSON Pointer strings, as JSON Patch requires, while Immer's paths are always arrays. A string path cannot name a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key.
* **Applying patches.** `apply()` takes the `enableAutoFreeze`, `strict` and `mark` options, or `mutable: true` to change the state in place and return `undefined`.
* **Alike in both.** `apply()` and `applyPatches()` change a draft in place, copy patch values before applying them, accept `-` as the index that appends to an array, and reject `move`, `copy` and `test` operations and paths through `__proto__` or `constructor`. As they copy patch values, an object that patches add to a Set is a copy, which the inverse patches cannot remove, so an undo after a redo leaves it in the Set in both libraries, and both append the elements that patches add, so such a Set can hold its elements in another order; see [Sets of objects](/docs/advanced-guides/patches#sets-of-objects).

## Immer behaviors that Mutative handles [#immer-behaviors-that-mutative-handles]

Mutative passes the test suite of Immer, adapted to its API. The [non-support tests](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/test/immer-non-support.test.ts) pin cases that Immer 11.1.18 gets wrong and Mutative does not, such as a draft that escapes into the next state and Map keys that stay mutable after freezing. The [array methods audit](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/test/immer-array-methods.md) reproduces patch ordering, base mutation and draft finalization failures of Immer's `enableArrayMethods()` plugin, with [reproduction tests](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/test/immer-array-methods.test.ts) that include plugin-disabled controls and run the same recipes against Mutative.

## Mutative vs Immer Performance [#mutative-vs-immer-performance]

With matched settings, both freezing or both not and both generating patches or both not, Mutative was faster than Immer 11.1.18 in 595 of 614 measured cases, 3.6x on geometric mean. With each library's defaults, Mutative without auto-freeze and Immer with it, Mutative was faster in 154 of 157 cases, 6.6x on geometric mean. Immer was faster only with auto-freeze: when updating class instances with many fields, and in two 100-row array updates whose runs overlapped those of Mutative.

With patches on and auto-freeze off, Mutative was faster in 148 of 150 cases and never slower, and faster in every array case: 4.4x Immer and 13x Mutative 1.3.0 on geometric mean. The comparisons run Immer without its `enableArrayMethods()` plugin. In Immer 11.1.18 the plugin returns raw base objects from `shift`, `pop` and `splice`, so editing them changes the previous state, and its patches can fail to replay; the audit above reproduces these failures.

Immer 11.0.0 ported the finalization callbacks of Mutative, which replace a recursive traversal of the draft tree, in [immerjs/immer#1183](https://github.com/immerjs/immer/pull/1183). Immer 11.1.18, which these measurements use, includes them.

See [Performance](/docs/getting-started/performance) for selected results, and the [performance summary](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/perf-testing/reports/SUMMARY.md) for the complete results, the method, and their limits.


# Contributing (/docs/extra-topics/contributing)

Set up the repository, run its checks, and contribute code, benchmarks and docs.

Mutative's goal is efficient immutable updates. The focus is on performance and on APIs that make development easier, and pull requests that help with either are welcome. For a larger change, open an [issue](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/issues) or a [discussion](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/discussions) first.

### Development Workflow [#development-workflow]

* Clone the [repository](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative), and use Node.js 22 or 24 with the pnpm version that `package.json` declares.
* Run `pnpm install` to install all the dependencies.
* Run `pnpm test` to run the tests, or `pnpm test --watch` for an interactive test watcher.
* Run `pnpm format`, `pnpm lint` and `pnpm type-check` before you commit.
* Run `pnpm commit` to write a commit message in the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/) format.
* Create a pull request.

### Builds, packages and benchmarks [#builds-packages-and-benchmarks]

[Building and validating Mutative](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/BUILDING.md) describes the build pipeline, the package checks, the bundle size limits and the generated API reference. [The benchmark suite](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/perf-testing/README.md) compares the current build with Mutative 1.3.0, Immer and hand-written reducers, and describes the regression budgets that CI checks: run `pnpm benchmark:immer:check` to validate every workload and `pnpm benchmark:immer` to measure them.

### Docs [#docs]

* The website lives in [`website/`](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/tree/main/website). Run `pnpm start:docs` from the repository root to preview it, and `pnpm build` in `website/` to export it and check its links.
* Code examples that import from `mutative`, and from no other module than `mutative` and `immer`, run as tests, with Vitest's `expect`: keep such examples complete, and leave the imports out of fragments that are not meant to run.
* `pnpm build:doc` regenerates the API reference in [`docs/`](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/tree/main/docs) from the TSDoc comments of the source, and CI checks that it is up to date.
* Write each Markdown paragraph and list item on a single line.


# Production error codes (/docs/extra-topics/errors)

Decode minified Mutative production errors, and find the errors and warnings of development builds.

In Mutative's minified production build, full error messages are replaced with numeric codes to reduce the number of bytes sent to users.

When debugging locally, we recommend using the development build. It retains the full error messages, additional validation, and warnings that provide more context about potential problems in your application; see [Development and production builds](/docs/getting-started/installation#development-and-production-builds).

If an exception occurs in production, its message reads `Minified Mutative error #<code>; visit https://mutative.js.org/docs/extra-topics/errors`. Find that code in the table below to recover the message that the development build throws, where `<…>` stands for a value of the call. The source identifier is provided for contributors working on Mutative itself.

Numeric codes remain stable when an error is removed. Retired codes are reserved so that older production logs can still be decoded.

| Code | Source identifier                | Development message                                                                                                          |
| ---: | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|    0 | `InvalidBaseState`               | `Invalid base state: create() only supports plain objects, arrays, Set, Map or using mark() to mark the state as immutable.` |
|    1 | `CannotAssignToMapOrSet`         | `Map/Set draft does not support any property assignment.`                                                                    |
|    2 | `InvalidArrayIndex`              | `Only supports setting array indices and the 'length' property.`                                                             |
|    3 | `CannotSetPrototypeOfDraft`      | `Cannot call 'setPrototypeOf()' on drafts`                                                                                   |
|    4 | `CannotDefinePropertyOnDraft`    | `Cannot call 'defineProperty()' on drafts`                                                                                   |
|    5 | `MutateAndReturn`                | `Either the value is returned as a new non-draft value, or only the draft is modified without returning any value.`          |
|    6 | `CannotReturnModifiedChildDraft` | `Cannot return a modified child draft.`                                                                                      |
|    7 | `CurrentOnNonDraft`              | `current() is only used for Draft, parameter: <value>`                                                                       |
|    8 | `StrictModeAccess`               | `Strict mode: Mutable data cannot be accessed directly, please use 'unsafe(callback)' wrap.`                                 |
|    9 | `UnsupportedMarkResult`          | `Unsupported mark result: <result>`                                                                                          |
|   10 | `InvalidMark`                    | `Please check mark() to ensure that it is a stable marker draftable function.`                                               |
|   11 | `CannotModifyFrozenObject`       | `Cannot modify frozen object`                                                                                                |
|   12 | `InvalidPatchPath` (retired)     | A generated patch path was invalid. This internal check has been removed; the code is reserved.                              |
|   13 | `ReservedPatchAttribute`         | `Patching reserved attributes like __proto__ and constructor is not allowed.`                                                |
|   14 | `CannotApplyPatch`               | `Cannot apply patch at '<path>'.`                                                                                            |
|   15 | `ReplacePatchOnSet`              | `Cannot apply replace patch to set.`                                                                                         |
|   16 | `UnsupportedPatchOperation`      | `Unsupported patch operation: <op>.`                                                                                         |
|   17 | `ApplyOptionsToDraft`            | `Cannot apply patches with options to a draft.`                                                                              |
|   18 | `OriginalOnNonDraft`             | `original() is only used for a draft, parameter: <value>`                                                                    |
|   19 | `RawReturnWithoutValue`          | `rawReturn() must be called with a value.`                                                                                   |
|   20 | `RawReturnWithExtraArguments`    | `rawReturn() must be called with one argument.`                                                                              |
|   21 | `ReplaceMutableRoot`             | `apply() with the mutable option changes the state in place, so a patch cannot replace the root state with another value.`   |

What the errors mean:

* **0**: the base state of `create()` is not draftable, such as a class instance or a `Date`; see [`isDraftable()`](/docs/api-reference/isdraftable) and [marks](/docs/advanced-guides/mark).
* **1–4**: a recipe assigned a property to a Map or Set draft, assigned a non-index property to an array draft, or called `Object.setPrototypeOf()` or `Object.defineProperty()` on a draft.
* **5** and **6**: a recipe changed its draft and returned another value, or returned a changed child draft; see [Returning a new state](/docs/api-reference/create#returning-a-new-state).
* **7** and **18**: `current()` or `original()` received a value that is not a draft.
* **8**: in [strict mode](/docs/advanced-guides/strict-mode), a recipe read a value that is not drafted outside `unsafe()`.
* **9**: a `mark` returned a value other than `'mutable'`, `'immutable'`, a function or nothing.
* **10**: a `mark` answered differently for the same value, such as `'immutable'` when Mutative drafted it and nothing when Mutative copied it; a mark must give the same answer for a value each time.
* **11**: code called `set()`, `add()`, `delete()` or `clear()` on a Map or Set that [auto-freeze](/docs/advanced-guides/auto-freeze) froze.
* **13–17** and **21**: `apply()` received a patch that it cannot apply; see [Patches that apply() accepts](/docs/api-reference/apply#patches-that-apply-accepts).
* **19** and **20**: `rawReturn()` was called without an argument or with more than one.

## Development-only errors [#development-only-errors]

Development builds also throw these errors, for checks that production builds skip:

| Message                                                                                                                                                                              | Cause                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Invalid options: <options>, 'options' should be an object.`                                                                                                                         | `create()` or `makeCreator()` received options that are not an object.                                                          |
| `Invalid mark: <mark>, 'mark' should be a function.`                                                                                                                                 | An array of marks holds a value that is not a function.                                                                         |
| `You can't use mark and patches or auto freeze together.`                                                                                                                            | A mark returned a copy function while patches or auto-freeze are on.                                                            |
| `Forbids circular reference`                                                                                                                                                         | With auto-freeze, the next state holds an object that holds itself; a longer message names the path of the object that repeats. |
| `Patches with string paths only support string Map keys and no symbol keys, got a key of type '<type>'. Set 'pathAsArray' to true to keep keys of other types.`                      | With `pathAsArray: false`, a patch path would hold a Map key that is not a string, or a symbol key.                             |
| `A draft cannot be a Map key: its producer revokes it when it ends. Use original(key), current(key) or an id as the key; see https://mutative.js.org/docs/extra-topics/faq`          | A recipe passed a draft to the `set()` method of a Map draft as the key.                                                        |
| `The return value holds a draft in a frozen object or in a value it holds. With auto-freeze, production builds do not search frozen objects for drafts, so do not put drafts there.` | With auto-freeze, a value that a recipe returned holds a draft inside a frozen object.                                          |

## Development warnings [#development-warnings]

Development builds print these warnings with `console.warn()`; production builds do not:

| Message                                                                                                                                                               | Cause                                                                                                                                                          |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `The return value does not contain any draft, please use 'rawReturn()' to wrap the return value to improve performance.`                                              | A recipe returned an object that holds no drafts, which [`rawReturn()`](/docs/api-reference/rawreturn) would return without searching it.                      |
| `The return value contains drafts, please don't use 'rawReturn()' to wrap the return value.`                                                                          | In strict mode, a value that `rawReturn()` wraps holds drafts.                                                                                                 |
| ``rawReturn() must be called with an object(including plain object, arrays, Set, Map, etc.) or `undefined`, other types do not need to be returned via rawReturn().`` | `rawReturn()` received a primitive, which a recipe can return as it is.                                                                                        |
| `Strict mode: the recipe left <count> drafts unchanged; …`                                                                                                            | Once, in strict mode, when a recipe leaves 1,000 or more drafts unchanged; see [searching a large array](/docs/api-reference/current#searching-a-large-array). |
| `create() received a draft as its base and drafts current(draft), unlike Immer's produce: …`                                                                          | Once, when `create()` receives a draft with a recipe; see [create() on a draft](/docs/api-reference/create#create-on-a-draft).                                 |
| `The "mutable" option is not allowed to be used with other options.`                                                                                                  | `apply()` received `mutable: true` together with other options.                                                                                                |


# FAQ (/docs/extra-topics/faq)

Answers to common questions about Mutative, its performance, migration from Immer, arrays, Maps and Sets.

For other questions, start a thread in [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/discussions), or open an [issue](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/issues) for a bug.

## Q\&A [#qa]

### Why does Mutative have such good performance? [#why-does-mutative-have-such-good-performance]

Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes a recipe makes, drafts only the values that a recipe reads, finalizes only the drafts that changed, and moves array elements natively on its copies instead of through the draft's proxy. It also leaves the next state unfrozen by default. See [Performance](/docs/getting-started/performance) for the measurements.

### I'm already using Immer, can I migrate smoothly to Mutative? [#im-already-using-immer-can-i-migrate-smoothly-to-mutative]

Yes. Unless you have to be compatible with Internet Explorer, Mutative supports almost all of Immer's features, and the [migration guide](/docs/advanced-guides/migration) shows how to replace each API. [Comparison with Immer](/docs/extra-topics/comparison-with-immer) lists the APIs that replace Immer's and every behavior that differs.

Mutative, like Immer, needs `Proxy`. On Android, React Native supports it since version 0.59 with JavaScriptCore and since version 0.64 with [Hermes](https://reactnative.dev/blog/2021/03/12/version-0.64#hermes-with-proxy-support).

### Can Mutative be integrated with Redux? [#can-mutative-be-integrated-with-redux]

Yes. A [producer](/docs/advanced-guides/currying) with an action argument is a reducer, and a recipe can return a new state, for example the initial state with [`rawReturn()`](/docs/api-reference/rawreturn). Redux Toolkit drafts state with Immer in `createSlice()` and `createReducer()`, and an RFC to make its [`produce()` configurable](https://github.com/reduxjs/redux-toolkit/pull/3074) is open.

### Which array methods run natively on drafts? [#which-array-methods-run-natively-on-drafts]

`shift`, `unshift`, `splice` and `reverse` move elements directly on the copy of a plain array without holes, including `undefined` elements; `indexOf`, `lastIndexOf` and `includes` search the current array natively; `sort` and `join` run natively on arrays of primitives. Removed elements are returned as drafts, patches replay in both directions, and a call that changes nothing keeps the state. Sparse arrays, array subclasses, an own `constructor` or `Symbol.isConcatSpreadable`, arrays under a custom `mark`, every method with a callback, `at`, `slice`, `fill` and `copyWithin` use the proxy path. An argument that can run user code, such as an object passed as `fromIndex` or as a `splice` index, is converted on the proxy path, so a conversion that changes the array is observed as the native methods observe it. The fast paths are made for data arrays: an accessor property defined on an array index is read as a data value, and the number and order of such getter calls, their re-entrant effects on the draft, and the identity of objects they return are not guaranteed to match element-by-element execution through the proxy. With auto-freeze, Mutative may also read such a getter twice when it copies a frozen, sealed or non-extensible array.

Optimized searches give the same results as the proxy path, comparing elements as a read returns them. Drafts, values assigned in the recipe, non-draftable objects and primitives are found. An object of the base state is drafted when it is read, so it is never found, whether or not it was read before, unless the recipe assigned or inserted it and it is not at its original index; use [`original()`](/docs/api-reference/original) to search the base state, for example `original(draft.list).indexOf(item)`. The search never reads a property of the value it is given.

In strict mode, outside [`unsafe()`](/docs/api-reference/unsafe), optimized calls on an array that may hold objects take the proxy path unchanged, so reading a non-draftable element fails exactly as it always did; arrays of primitives, recognized with `typeof` alone, keep the native paths. Elements are moved and compared without being inspected, while the proxy path inspects each element it reads. An element that is itself a Proxy may therefore see fewer calls to its internal methods on the native paths, never more and never at other times; a revoked Proxy element that a search passes over, for example, does not throw there.

Draftable base elements removed or moved by these methods are drafted before they are exposed. Methods with callbacks, such as `forEach`, `map`, `filter` and `find`, go through the draft so that their callbacks see every change and can modify elements; use [`current()`](/docs/api-reference/current) for read-only scans of large arrays.

### Can a recipe change a Map draft while iterating over it? [#can-a-recipe-change-a-map-draft-while-iterating-over-it]

Yes. Deleting the entry being visited and changing the values of other entries work as on a Map, and Set drafts iterate like Sets. One difference remains: an iteration over a Map draft that starts before the recipe has changed that Map, or read an object value from it, walks the entries of the base Map. An entry that the recipe deletes later in such an iteration is still visited, with `undefined` as its value, and an entry that it adds is not visited. To delete other entries while iterating, iterate over `Array.from(draft.keys())` and skip the keys for which `draft.has()` returns false.

### Do the Set methods such as `union()` and `isSubsetOf()` work on Set drafts? [#do-the-set-methods-such-as-union-and-issubsetof-work-on-set-drafts]

Yes, but they compare elements as iterating the draft returns them. An object of the base state is a draft there, so these methods do not match it with the original object, although `has()` accepts the original object. To compare a Set draft with objects of the base state, call the method on `current(draft)`, in which unchanged objects keep their identity, or on `original(draft)` for the base state, or compare ids, for example `[...draft].filter((item) => ids.has(item.id))`. This applies to `union()`, `intersection()`, `difference()`, `symmetricDifference()`, `isSubsetOf()`, `isSupersetOf()` and `isDisjointFrom()`.

### Can a draft be a Map key? [#can-a-draft-be-a-map-key]

No. Map keys are used as they are, and a draft is revoked when its producer ends, so a Map that kept a draft as a key, and the patches that name that key, would hold a revoked draft, whose properties throw when they are read. Use `original(draft)`, `current(draft)` or an id as the key. Development builds throw when a recipe passes a draft to the `set()` method of a Map draft.

### Does Mutative support shared references? [#does-mutative-support-shared-references]

Yes, Mutative supports shared references, but **each path to a shared object gets its own independent draft**. Modifications to one path do not automatically reflect in others. If you want to preserve shared references in the result, you must explicitly assign them (e.g., `draft.b = draft.a`). [Read more details](/docs/extra-topics/shared-references).

### Can I keep a draft after the recipe ends? [#can-i-keep-a-draft-after-the-recipe-ends]

No. Mutative revokes the drafts of a `create()` call when its recipe ends, also when it fails, so reading a draft afterwards throws. Keep [`current(draft)`](/docs/api-reference/current), a snapshot of plain values, or the next state instead. A draft of a [manual `create(base)`](/docs/advanced-guides/currying#drafts-that-you-finalize-later) lives until `finalize()` returns, and the draft of an async recipe until its Promise settles.
