# Mutative Ecosystem (/docs/extra-topics/mutative-ecosystem)

Libraries built on Mutative for React, Zustand, Jotai, XState, Yjs, undo and redo, and more.

These libraries use Mutative for the immutable updates of other tools. Install each one together with `mutative`, and see its repository for its full API.

## React [#react]

* [use-mutative](https://github.com/mutativejs/use-mutative) - A 2-6x faster alternative to useState with spread operation, with `useMutative()` and `useMutativeReducer()`; see [Using Mutative with React](/docs/getting-started/mutative-with-react).
* [use-travel](https://github.com/mutativejs/use-travel) - A React hook for state time travel with undo, redo, reset and archive functionalities.
* [reactant](https://github.com/unadlib/reactant) - A framework for building React applications, with Mutative for immutable updates.

## Zustand [#zustand]

[zustand-mutative](https://github.com/mutativejs/zustand-mutative) is a Mutative middleware for Zustand, whose `set()` then takes a recipe:

```tsx
import { create } from 'zustand';
import { mutative } from 'zustand-mutative';

type State = { count: number };
type Actions = { increment: (qty: number) => void };

export const useCountStore = create<State & Actions>()(
  mutative((set) => ({
    count: 0,
    increment: (qty) =>
      set((state) => {
        state.count += qty;
      }),
  }))
);
```

[zustand-travel](https://github.com/mutativejs/zustand-travel) is an undo and redo middleware for Zustand, built on travels.

## Jotai [#jotai]

[jotai-mutative](https://github.com/mutativejs/jotai-mutative) provides atoms whose setters take a recipe:

```tsx
import { useAtom } from 'jotai';
import { atomWithMutative } from 'jotai-mutative';

const countAtom = atomWithMutative({ value: 0 });

export function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useAtom(countAtom);
  return (
    <button
      onClick={() =>
        setCount((draft) => {
          draft.value += 1;
        })
      }
    >
      {count.value}
    </button>
  );
}
```

`withMutative(atom)` and `useMutativeAtom(atom)` give existing atoms the same setter.

## XState [#xstate]

[xstate-mutative](https://github.com/mutativejs/xstate-mutative) provides an `assign()` action for XState 5 that changes a draft of the context:

```ts
import { createActor, createMachine } from 'xstate';
import { assign } from 'xstate-mutative';

const machine = createMachine({
  context: { count: 0 },
  on: {
    increment: {
      actions: assign(({ context }) => {
        context.count += 1;
      }),
    },
  },
});

const actor = createActor(machine).start();
actor.send({ type: 'increment' });
```

## Undo and redo [#undo-and-redo]

[travels](https://github.com/mutativejs/travels) is a framework-agnostic undo and redo core that keeps the history of a state as Mutative patches, with history limits, archives and persistence:

```ts
import { createTravels } from 'travels';

const travels = createTravels({ count: 0 });

travels.setState((draft) => {
  draft.count += 1;
});
travels.back();
travels.forward();
```

[use-travel](https://github.com/mutativejs/use-travel) and [zustand-travel](https://github.com/mutativejs/zustand-travel) bring it to React and Zustand. To build undo and redo on patches yourself, see [Patches](/docs/advanced-guides/patches#undo-and-redo).

## Collaboration [#collaboration]

[mutative-yjs](https://github.com/mutativejs/mutative-yjs) binds a Yjs `Y.Map` or `Y.Array` to a plain snapshot, which recipes update and remote changes refresh:

```ts
import * as Y from 'yjs';
import { bind } from 'mutative-yjs';

const doc = new Y.Doc();
const binder = bind<{ count: number; items: string[] }>(doc.getMap('data'));

binder.update((state) => {
  state.count = 0;
  state.items = ['apple'];
});
binder.update((state) => {
  state.count += 1;
  state.items.push('banana');
});

binder.get(); // { count: 1, items: ['apple', 'banana'] }
```

## Other libraries [#other-libraries]

* [mutative-compat](https://github.com/exuanbo/mutative-compat) - Mutative wrapper with full Immer API compatibility.
* [mutability](https://github.com/mutativejs/mutability) - A JavaScript library for transactional mutable updates, which changes the state in place and returns patches.
* [usm](https://github.com/reactant/usm) - A concise and flexible state model for Redux, MobX, Vuex, Pinia and more.
* [coaction](https://github.com/coactionjs/coaction) - An immutable reactive state runtime for TypeScript.
* [coexist](https://github.com/coactionjs/coexist) - The application runtime for coexisting UI frameworks.


# Shared References (/docs/extra-topics/shared-references)

How Mutative drafts an object that several paths of the state lead to, and how to keep it shared.

Mutative supports non-unidirectional trees (DAGs with shared nodes) where there is more than one path from the root to the same node, **as long as there are no cycles**. However, there is an important behavior to understand regarding how drafts handle these shared references.

## Independent Drafts for Multiple Paths [#independent-drafts-for-multiple-paths]

When the same object is referenced from multiple paths in the base state, Mutative creates **independent drafts for each path**. This means modifications to one path will **not** automatically reflect in the other paths.

```javascript
import { create } from 'mutative';

const obj = {};
// Same object referenced by two keys
obj.color1 = obj.color2 = { name: 'Red' };

const result = create(obj, (draft) => {
  // ⚠️ Different drafts created for each path!
  console.log(draft.color1 === draft.color2); // false

  draft.color1.name = 'Blue';
  
  // color2 remains unchanged because it has a separate draft
  console.log(draft.color2.name); // 'Red'
});

console.log(result.color1 === result.color2); // false
// Result: { color1: { name: 'Blue' }, color2: { name: 'Red' } }
```

This behavior is **by design** and matches Immer's behavior. Each path through the state tree gets its own independent draft proxy.

## Creating Shared References [#creating-shared-references]

If you need to **preserve or create shared references** in the result state, you must do so explicitly within your recipe function by assigning one draft to another.

```javascript
const result = create(obj, (draft) => {
  draft.color1.name = 'Blue';
  
  // ✅ Explicitly share the reference
  draft.color2 = draft.color1;
});

// Now they share the same reference in the result
console.log(result.color1 === result.color2); // true
// Result: { color1: { name: 'Blue' }, color2: { name: 'Blue' } }
```

## Summary [#summary]

| Scenario                         | Behavior                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Shared nodes in base state**   | Each path gets its own **independent draft**. Mutations through one path do **not** reflect in other paths. |
| **Manually assigned references** | ✅ **Supported**. Assigning `draft.x = draft.y` creates shared references in the final state.                |
| **Real cycles**                  | ❌ **Not supported**. Cycles are actively detected in development mode when auto-freeze is enabled.          |


# Who Uses Mutative (/docs/extra-topics/who-uses-mutative)

Open-source projects that replaced Immer with Mutative, and what they reported.

These open-source projects depend on Mutative directly. The quotes come from the pull requests and release notes in which they adopted it, and each describes that project at that time, not every workload. The projects were checked against their default branches on October 9, 2026.

## Appsmith [#appsmith]

[Appsmith](https://github.com/appsmithorg/appsmith), a platform to build admin panels, internal tools and dashboards, replaced Immer with Mutative in its client:

> Using mutative instead of immer, this has reduced the main thread scripting by about 1 second.

From [appsmithorg/appsmith#38993](https://github.com/appsmithorg/appsmith/pull/38993), merged on February 6, 2025. The same pull request also removed a deep clone and skipped Mutative for the first evaluation of its tree.

## InstantDB [#instantdb]

[InstantDB](https://github.com/instantdb/instant), a backend with auth, permissions, storage and presence, replaced Immer with Mutative, which does not rely on auto-freeze. In its performance tester, a single transaction took about 8 ms with Immer, and about 40 ms as pending transactions were added:

> Mutative is about 3ms on a single transaction. As I add more pending transactions, the size *seems to stay* at 3ms!

From [instantdb/instant#243](https://github.com/instantdb/instant/pull/243), merged on September 19, 2024.

## Notesnook [#notesnook]

[Notesnook](https://github.com/streetwriters/notesnook), an end-to-end encrypted note-taking app, replaced Immer with Mutative in version 3.0.11:

> we have gotten rid of immer and replaced it with mutative for immutable state management inside the app. mutative is almost 10x faster so you'll notice slight improvements in app responsiveness.

From the [Notesnook v3.0.11 release notes](https://notesnook.com/blog/notesnook-v3.0.11), July 18, 2024. The 10x figure describes the library; for the app, the release notes speak of slight improvements in responsiveness.

## Plate [#plate]

[Plate](https://github.com/udecode/plate), a rich-text editor for React, moved its plugin stores to [zustand-mutative](https://github.com/mutativejs/zustand-mutative) in version 42, and its core package depends on Mutative:

> All plugin stores now use zustand-mutative for immutable state updates, which is faster than `immer`.

From the [release of version 42](https://github.com/udecode/plate/pull/3945), merged on January 9, 2025.

## Also used by [#also-used-by]

* [Mol\*](https://github.com/molstar/molstar), a comprehensive macromolecular library, replaced Immer with Mutative in [molstar/molstar#1618](https://github.com/molstar/molstar/pull/1618), together with other optimizations of its animation loading.
* [OpenRewrite](https://github.com/openrewrite/rewrite), for automated mass refactoring of source code, replaced Immer with Mutative in its JavaScript support in [openrewrite/rewrite#6460](https://github.com/openrewrite/rewrite/pull/6460).
* [MSW Data](https://github.com/mswjs/data), a data querying library for testing JavaScript applications.


# Concepts (/docs/getting-started/concepts)

Drafts, finalization with structural sharing, patches and marks, the ideas behind Mutative.

Mutative is based on `Proxy`. A recipe changes a draft of the state, Mutative records which parts changed, and it produces the next state from those changes, sharing every part that did not change. Patches describe the changes, and marks decide which values are drafted.

## Base Workflow [#base-workflow]

<img alt="Mutative workflow" src="__img0" />

* The current state is the base state, which never changes.
* The draft is where the recipe makes its changes. Mutative creates a draft of each object that the recipe reads, shown with dotted lines, and copies the objects that it changes, shown in red.
* The next state holds the copies of the changed objects and shares all the others with the base state.

```ts
import { create, isDraft } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  a0: {
    b0: {},
  },
  a1: {
    b1: {},
    b2: {
      c0: 0,
    },
  },
  a2: {},
};

const nextState = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  const { a0 } = draft;
  // Reading a draftable value through a draft gives a draft of it.
  expect(isDraft(a0)).toBe(true);
  draft.a1.b2.c0 = 1;
});

expect(nextState).not.toBe(baseState);
// Drafted but not changed: shared with the base state.
expect(nextState.a0).toBe(baseState.a0);
// Never read: shared with the base state.
expect(nextState.a2).toBe(baseState.a2);
// Changed, and every object on the path to the change: copied.
expect(nextState.a1).not.toBe(baseState.a1);
expect(nextState.a1.b2).not.toBe(baseState.a1.b2);
expect(nextState.a1.b1).toBe(baseState.a1.b1);
expect(nextState.a1.b2.c0).toBe(1);
```

## Drafts [#drafts]

A draft is a `Proxy` of a value of the state. It behaves like that value: a recipe reads it, assigns to it, deletes from it and calls its methods, such as `push()` on arrays or `set()` on Maps. Mutative drafts lazily:

* Reading a draftable value through a draft gives a draft of it, created on that first read. Plain objects, arrays, Maps and Sets are draftable, and so are the values that a [mark](/docs/advanced-guides/mark) makes draftable, such as class instances; see [`isDraftable()`](/docs/api-reference/isdraftable). Other values, such as primitives and dates, are returned as they are.
* The first change to a draft makes a shallow copy of its value, and later changes go to the same copy, so Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes the recipe makes.
* Values that the recipe assigns are not drafted: the next state holds them as they are.
* Each path to an object gets a draft of its own, also when several paths lead to the same object; see [Shared references](/docs/extra-topics/shared-references).

Drafts live only as long as their `create()` call: when the recipe ends, Mutative revokes them, and reading one later throws. Keep [`current(draft)`](/docs/api-reference/current), a snapshot of plain values, instead of a draft, and check for drafts with [`isDraft()`](/docs/api-reference/isdraft).

## Finalization [#finalization]

When the recipe ends, Mutative finalizes the drafts: the next state holds the copy of each changed draft and the original value of every unchanged one, so it shares every object that the recipe did not change with the base state. A recipe that changes nothing returns the base state itself. With [auto-freeze](/docs/advanced-guides/auto-freeze), Mutative then freezes the next state deeply.

A recipe can also return a new state instead of changing the draft; see [Returning a new state](/docs/api-reference/create#returning-a-new-state).

## Patches [#patches]

With the `enablePatches` option, `create()` also returns patches, which describe the changes of the recipe, and inverse patches, which undo them. Each patch is an object with an `op`, `add`, `remove` or `replace`, a `path` from the root to the changed value, and, for `add` and `replace`, the new `value`. [`apply()`](/docs/api-reference/apply) applies patches to a state, for example to replay changes on another copy of the state or to undo them; see [Patches](/docs/advanced-guides/patches).

## Mark [#mark]

A state can mix data that should be drafted with data that should not, such as class instances, caches or values from other libraries. The `mark` option decides, value by value, whether Mutative drafts a value, leaves it mutable, or copies it with a function of your own, without marking the objects themselves. See [Marking data structure](/docs/advanced-guides/mark).


# Getting Started (/docs/getting-started)

5 minutes to learn the most important Mutative concepts.

- [Installation](/docs/getting-started/installation)
- [Usages](/docs/getting-started/usages)
- [Concepts](/docs/getting-started/concepts)
- [Using Mutative with React](/docs/getting-started/mutative-with-react)
- [Performance](/docs/getting-started/performance)


# Installation (/docs/getting-started/installation)

Install Mutative from npm or load it from a CDN, and check the environments it supports.

## Package managers [#package-managers]



```bash
npm install mutative
```

```bash
pnpm add mutative
```

```bash
yarn add mutative
```

```bash
bun add mutative
```

Mutative has no dependencies. A production bundle of `create` alone is about 7.9 kB after Brotli compression, and one of `create`, `apply`, `current` and `original` about 8.5 kB, including patches, `Map` and `Set` support and native array methods, which need no plugins.

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';
```

## Requirements [#requirements]

* **JavaScript.** Mutative needs `Proxy` and the ES2018 syntax that its builds keep, such as object spread: Node.js 14.0 or later, current browsers, and React Native 0.64 or later. Engines that support `Proxy` but not ES2018 syntax, such as Chrome 49–59, Firefox 18–54, Safari 10–11.0 and Edge 12–18, need Mutative transpiled by your build. Internet Explorer has no `Proxy` and is not supported.
* **TypeScript.** The type declarations support TypeScript 5.0 and later; see [TypeScript](/docs/advanced-guides/typescript).

## Development and production builds [#development-and-production-builds]

The package holds a development build, with full error messages, warnings and extra checks, and a minified production build, whose errors are [numeric codes](/docs/extra-topics/errors). Which one runs depends on `process.env.NODE_ENV`:

* **Bundlers** resolve the ESM build, whose development checks compare `process.env.NODE_ENV` with `'production'`. Bundlers that define it as `'production'`, as webpack, Vite, Rollup and esbuild setups for production usually do, drop the development code. Bundles that target Node.js resolve the CommonJS entry instead; define `process.env.NODE_ENV` there, or leave Mutative external.
* **Node.js** runs the CommonJS build for `require` and `import` alike, and selects the development or production build from `NODE_ENV` when it loads Mutative.
* **Browsers without a bundler** have no `process`, so they need the production ESM file or the UMD build below.

## CDN [#cdn]

* Unpkg: `<script src="https://unpkg.com/mutative"></script>`
* JSDelivr: `<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mutative"></script>`
* ES module: `import { create } from 'https://unpkg.com/mutative/dist/mutative.esm.production.min.mjs';`

The `<script>` tags load the production UMD build, which defines a global `Mutative`, as in `Mutative.create(baseState, recipe)`. The package's other ESM files read `process.env.NODE_ENV`, which bundlers and Node.js provide; a browser without a bundler needs the production file above.

```html
<script type="module">
  import { create } from 'https://unpkg.com/mutative/dist/mutative.esm.production.min.mjs';

  const state = create({ count: 0 }, (draft) => {
    draft.count += 1;
  });
  console.log(state.count); // 1
</script>
```


# Using Mutative with React (/docs/getting-started/mutative-with-react)

Update React state with create(), or with the use-mutative hooks.

React re-renders when a component's state is replaced with a new object, so state updates must not change the current state. `create()` produces that new state from changes to a draft, and the parts of the state that a recipe leaves unchanged keep their references, so memoized children and selectors skip them.

## With `useState` and `useReducer` [#with-usestate-and-usereducer]

`create()` needs no adapter: call it in a functional update of `useState`, or in a reducer for `useReducer`.

```tsx
import { useReducer, useState } from 'react';
import { create } from 'mutative';

type Todo = { text: string; done: boolean };

export function TodoList() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState<Todo[]>([{ text: 'Learn React', done: false }]);

  const toggle = (index: number) =>
    setTodos((current) =>
      create(current, (draft) => {
        draft[index].done = !draft[index].done;
      })
    );

  return (
    <ul>
      {todos.map((todo, index) => (
        <li key={index} onClick={() => toggle(index)}>
          {todo.done ? '✓' : '○'} {todo.text}
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

type Action = { type: 'add'; text: string } | { type: 'remove'; index: number };

function reducer(state: Todo[], action: Action) {
  return create(state, (draft) => {
    switch (action.type) {
      case 'add':
        draft.push({ text: action.text, done: false });
        break;
      case 'remove':
        draft.splice(action.index, 1);
        break;
    }
  });
}

export function useTodos(initialTodos: Todo[]) {
  return useReducer(reducer, initialTodos);
}
```

A recipe that changes nothing returns the current state itself, so React skips the re-render.

## use-mutative [#use-mutative]

[use-mutative](https://github.com/mutativejs/use-mutative) wraps these patterns in two hooks.



```bash
npm install mutative use-mutative
```

```bash
pnpm add mutative use-mutative
```

```bash
yarn add mutative use-mutative
```

```bash
bun add mutative use-mutative
```

### `useMutative()` [#usemutative]

`useMutative()` works like `useState()`, and its setter also takes a recipe that changes a draft:

```tsx
import { useMutative } from 'use-mutative';

export function App() {
  const [state, setState] = useMutative({
    foo: 'bar',
    list: [{ text: 'todo' }],
  });

  return (
    <>
      <button
        onClick={() => {
          // Change a draft of the state.
          setState((draft) => {
            draft.foo = `${draft.foo} 2`;
            draft.list.push({ text: 'todo 2' });
          });
        }}
      >
        Update
      </button>
      <button
        onClick={() => {
          // Or replace the state.
          setState({ foo: 'bar 2', list: [{ text: 'todo 2' }] });
        }}
      >
        Replace
      </button>
      <pre>{JSON.stringify(state, null, 2)}</pre>
    </>
  );
}
```

### `useMutativeReducer()` [#usemutativereducer]

`useMutativeReducer()` works like `useReducer()`, and its reducer receives a draft of the state. A reducer changes the draft and returns nothing, or returns a new state; wrap a returned value that holds no drafts in [`rawReturn()`](/docs/api-reference/rawreturn) to skip searching it for drafts.

```tsx
import { rawReturn, type Draft } from 'mutative';
import { useMutativeReducer } from 'use-mutative';

const initialState = { count: 0 };

type Action = { type: 'reset' | 'increment' | 'decrement' };

function reducer(draft: Draft<typeof initialState>, action: Action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'reset':
      return rawReturn(initialState);
    case 'increment':
      draft.count += 1;
      return;
    case 'decrement':
      draft.count -= 1;
      return;
  }
}

export function Counter() {
  const [state, dispatch] = useMutativeReducer(reducer, initialState);

  return (
    <div>
      Count: {state.count}
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'increment' })}>Increment</button>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'decrement' })}>Decrement</button>
      <button onClick={() => dispatch({ type: 'reset' })}>Reset</button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

### Options and patches [#options-and-patches]

Both hooks take the [options of `create()`](/docs/api-reference/create#options) as their last argument. With `enablePatches`, they also return the patches and inverse patches of the last update:

```tsx
const [state, setState, patches, inversePatches] = useMutative(initialState, {
  enablePatches: true,
});

const [state, dispatch, patches, inversePatches] = useMutativeReducer(
  reducer,
  initialState,
  undefined,
  { enablePatches: true }
);
```

The third argument of `useMutativeReducer()` is the optional initializer of `useReducer()`.

## Undo and redo [#undo-and-redo]

[use-travel](https://github.com/mutativejs/use-travel) keeps a history of the state from the patches of each update, with undo, redo and reset:

```tsx
import { useTravel } from 'use-travel';

export function Counter() {
  const [state, setState, controls] = useTravel({ count: 0 });

  return (
    <div>
      <strong>{state.count}</strong>
      <button
        onClick={() =>
          setState((draft) => {
            draft.count += 1;
          })
        }
      >
        Increment
      </button>
      <button onClick={() => controls.back()} disabled={!controls.canUndo}>
        Undo
      </button>
      <button onClick={() => controls.forward()} disabled={!controls.canRedo}>
        Redo
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}
```

State libraries such as Zustand, Jotai and XState have Mutative integrations as well; see the [ecosystem](/docs/extra-topics/mutative-ecosystem).


# Performance (/docs/getting-started/performance)

Benchmark results against Immer and hand-written reducers across 97 workloads, and how to run the benchmarks.

Mutative is about 3.6x faster than Immer with matched settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults, across 97 benchmarked workloads. A hand-written reducer that copies only what it changes is faster still in most of them.

## Benchmark suite [#benchmark-suite]

The [benchmark suite](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/tree/main/perf-testing) times 99 workloads: Immer's own performance tests, array methods, reads, Map and Set values, object records, class instances, a deep path, patch application, returned values, and searches. Its last full run measured 97 of them, and a focused run the two that return fresh data. It compares Mutative with Immer 11.1.18 and with reducers written by hand, after checking every result against those reducers. The [performance summary](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/perf-testing/reports/SUMMARY.md) has the complete results, the method, and their limits.

## Mutative vs Immer [#mutative-vs-immer]

> Mutative passed all of Immer's test cases.

With matched settings, both freezing or both not and both generating patches or both not, Mutative was faster than Immer in 595 of 614 measured cases, 3.6x on geometric mean. With each library's defaults, Mutative without auto-freeze and Immer with it, Mutative was faster in 154 of 157 cases, 6.6x on geometric mean. The other 3 return a state that Immer froze earlier: Immer skips frozen values when it searches a returned state for drafts, while Mutative, which does not freeze by default, searches it unless the recipe wraps it in [`rawReturn()`](/docs/api-reference/rawreturn#performance-compared-with-immer), which took 0.26 µs.

<PerformanceOverview />

Times are microseconds per update, medians of three runs on an Apple M1 Max with Node.js 24.16.0, each library in a process of its own; lower is better. Mutative, the first Immer column, and the hand-written reducers run without auto-freeze; the second Immer column shows Immer's default.

| Workload                            |   Rows | Mutative |  Immer | Immer, auto-freeze | Hand-written |
| ----------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | -----: | -----------------: | -----------: |
| Update one field of a small object  |      — |     0.51 |   0.69 |               0.95 |         0.02 |
| Update an array item found by ID    |    100 |     1.12 |   1.82 |               25.0 |         0.38 |
| 200 RTK Query-style updates         |      — |    1,001 |  1,133 |              4,795 |          352 |
| Read every row by index             | 10,000 |    4,756 |  9,584 |              9,687 |         57.7 |
| Remove the first row                | 10,000 |     7.04 |  7,408 |              8,137 |         1.40 |
| Update every row                    | 10,000 |    6,462 | 12,570 |             15,607 |          211 |
| Update one of 10,000 records        | 10,000 |    1,200 |  2,094 |              3,131 |        2,088 |
| Insert into a 1,000-property object |      — |     50.3 |    149 |                229 |          126 |
| Update a Map value                  | 10,000 |      518 |    526 |                733 |          519 |
| Add a number to a Set               | 10,000 |     29.5 |    904 |                975 |         61.2 |
| Update a class instance             | 10,000 |     2.92 |   3.44 |                668 |         1.42 |
| Update a value ten levels deep      |      — |     3.50 |   4.41 |               7.84 |         0.76 |
| Apply patches to 10% of rows        | 10,000 |      734 |  1,166 |              2,095 |            — |
| Search `current()` after `shift()`  | 10,000 |      257 | 11,255 |             11,846 |         64.8 |
| Return draft.filter()               | 10,000 |    2,658 |  4,251 |              4,736 |         77.7 |
| Return a new state                  | 10,000 |    2,604 |  5,718 |               0.79 |         0.02 |
| Return it with rawReturn()          | 10,000 |     0.26 |  5,703 |               0.79 |         0.02 |

Each library ran each workload in a process of its own. With all of them in one process every library ran slower, and not by the same amount: Mutative took 1.1 times as long on geometric mean, Immer 1.2 times, and the hand-written reducers 1.7 times. The search removes the first row with `shift()`, then finds the last row in a snapshot of the array and updates it. Immer has no `rawReturn()` and returns the same plain value in the last two rows; with auto-freeze, Mutative skips a returned state that is already frozen, as Immer does, taking 0.53 µs. Immer was faster in 6 of the 614 matched cases, all with auto-freeze: four updates of class instances with 100 to 10,000 fields, and two array updates at 100 rows whose runs overlapped those of Mutative.

## Large arrays [#large-arrays]

At 1,000 and 10,000 rows the gap grows. Against Immer without its array-method plugin, Mutative was faster in 222 of 232 cases at these sizes, 4.7x on geometric mean, and faster in every case that moves elements:

<ArrayScalingChart />

| Auto-freeze | Patches | All workloads, 1,000 rows | All workloads, 10,000 rows | Moves, 1,000 rows | Moves, 10,000 rows |
| ----------- | ------- | ------------------------: | -------------------------: | ----------------: | -----------------: |
| off         | off     |                      8.7x |                      10.8x |              209x |               430x |
| off         | on      |                      4.1x |                       4.5x |              7.1x |               7.3x |
| on          | off     |                      3.9x |                       4.2x |               32x |                39x |
| on          | on      |                      2.7x |                       2.8x |              6.6x |               6.8x |

Each value is the geometric mean of Immer's time over Mutative's; moves are `shift`, `unshift`, `splice` insertion, and `reverse`. Mutative moves elements natively on its copy, while Immer moves each one through its draft proxy: removing the first of 10,000 rows took 7.04 µs against 7,408 µs, 1,052x. With patches, both libraries emit one patch per moved index, which bounds the gain to 5-9x. The [performance summary](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/perf-testing/reports/SUMMARY.md) breaks these results down by scenario.

## With patches [#with-patches]

With patches on and auto-freeze off, Mutative was faster than Immer in 148 of 150 cases and within 5% in the other 2, 3.3x on geometric mean, and faster than Mutative 1.3.0 in 131 and within 5% in the rest, 4.6x. In every array case measured it was faster than both: 4.4x Immer and 13x Mutative 1.3.0 on geometric mean. Patches cost little when an update changes a few paths: pushing a row and inserting a property at 10,000 rows took 63.2 µs with patches against 63.8 µs without. Moving elements emits one patch per moved index in every library, so removing the first of 10,000 rows produces 10,000 forward and 10,000 inverse patches.

Times are microseconds per update with patches on and auto-freeze off:

<PatchComparisonChart />

| Workload                           |   Rows | Mutative |  Immer | Mutative 1.3.0 |
| ---------------------------------- | -----: | -------: | -----: | -------------: |
| Push a row and insert a property   | 10,000 |     63.2 |    360 |            210 |
| Update an array item found by ID   |    100 |     1.50 |   3.22 |           3.35 |
| 200 RTK Query-style updates        |      — |    1,140 |  1,470 |          2,116 |
| Remove the first row with `splice` |    100 |     11.5 |   83.6 |          2,982 |
| Insert a row in the middle         |    100 |     8.83 |   48.0 |          1,191 |
| Sort rows                          |    100 |      105 |    129 |          2,466 |
| Remove the first row with `shift`  | 10,000 |    1,063 |  8,943 |        265,439 |
| Reverse the rows                   | 10,000 |    1,071 |  9,424 |        280,542 |
| Update every row                   | 10,000 |    8,555 | 21,767 |         22,549 |
| Update one of 10,000 records       | 10,000 |    1,184 |  2,104 |          1,181 |

Immer's optional `enableArrayMethods()` plugin also runs array methods on the draft's copy, and with patches it comes within 1.13-1.70x of Mutative when moving elements of 1,000 or 10,000 rows. These comparisons leave it off because in Immer 11.1.18 it breaks guarantees that Immer otherwise keeps: `shift`, `pop` and `splice` return raw base objects, so editing a removed object changes the previous state; reordering can expose original objects the same way and leave revoked drafts in the result; and its forward patches can fail to replay. In [the audit](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/test/immer-array-methods.md), 123 of 4,913 three-step operation sequences break with the plugin and none without it. The [performance summary](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/perf-testing/reports/SUMMARY.md) reports Immer with the plugin separately.

## Mutative vs hand-written reducers [#mutative-vs-hand-written-reducers]

A hand-written reducer that copies only what it changes is faster than any library that drafts state, and it was faster than Mutative in 129 of the suite's 150 cases. Mutative was faster when copying wide objects, such as records with 1,000 keys or class instances with 100 fields, by 1.5-2.8x, when inserting at the front of 10,000 rows: 16 µs instead of 28 µs, and when adding a number to a Set of 1,000 or 10,000 numbers, which it copies faster than `new Set()` does: 30 µs instead of 61 µs at 10,000.

Spreads also become slow when code copies the same structure again and again. Mutative copies each object at most once per update, however many changes a recipe makes.

See [Performance tips](/docs/advanced-guides/performance-tips) for recipes that avoid needless drafts, searches, copies, freezing and patches.

## Run the benchmarks [#run-the-benchmarks]

From a clone of the repository:

```sh
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
pnpm benchmark:immer:check
pnpm benchmark:immer
```

The [benchmark guide](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/perf-testing/README.md) describes the workloads, options, memory measurements, and CI regression budgets.


# Usages (/docs/getting-started/usages)

Common immutable updates of objects, arrays, Maps and Sets with create().

## Use `create()` to create a new state [#use-create-to-create-a-new-state]

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  foo: 'bar',
  list: [{ text: 'coding' }],
};

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.list.push({ text: 'learning' });
});

expect(state).not.toBe(baseState);
expect(state.list).not.toBe(baseState.list);
expect(state.list[0]).toBe(baseState.list[0]);
```

`create(baseState, recipe, options?)` drafts the base state and passes the draft to the recipe. The recipe changes the draft with ordinary JavaScript, and `create()` returns the next state, which copies the objects that the recipe changed and shares all the others with the base state. The base state does not change. See [`create()`](/docs/api-reference/create) for its options and its other forms.

The examples below change a draft as plain JavaScript would change the state itself.

## Objects [#objects]

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  user: { name: 'Ada', address: { city: 'London' } },
  flags: { beta: true } as Record<string, boolean>,
};

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  // Update a nested property.
  draft.user.address.city = 'Paris';
  // Add a property.
  draft.flags.darkMode = true;
  // Delete a property.
  delete draft.flags.beta;
});

expect(state).toEqual({
  user: { name: 'Ada', address: { city: 'Paris' } },
  flags: { darkMode: true },
});
```

## Arrays [#arrays]

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

type Todo = { id: number; text: string; done: boolean };

const baseState: Todo[] = [
  { id: 1, text: 'learn', done: false },
  { id: 2, text: 'build', done: false },
  { id: 3, text: 'ship', done: false },
];

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  // Update the item with an id.
  const todo = draft.find((item) => item.id === 2);
  if (todo) todo.done = true;

  // Remove the item with an id.
  const index = draft.findIndex((item) => item.id === 1);
  if (index !== -1) draft.splice(index, 1);

  // Insert at the front, and add at the end.
  draft.unshift({ id: 0, text: 'plan', done: true });
  draft.push({ id: 4, text: 'celebrate', done: false });

  // Move the last item to the second position.
  const [moved] = draft.splice(draft.length - 1, 1);
  draft.splice(1, 0, moved);
});

expect(state.map((todo) => todo.id)).toEqual([0, 4, 2, 3]);
expect(state[2].done).toBe(true);
// Unchanged items keep their references.
expect(state[3]).toBe(baseState[2]);
```

To filter an array, assign the filtered array to the draft. Mutative replaces the drafts that the new array holds with their values:

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = { todos: [{ text: 'learn', done: true }, { text: 'ship', done: false }] };

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  draft.todos = draft.todos.filter((todo) => !todo.done);
});

expect(state.todos).toEqual([{ text: 'ship', done: false }]);
expect(state.todos[0]).toBe(baseState.todos[1]);
```

`find()`, `filter()` and other methods with callbacks visit the elements through the draft, so each element they visit becomes a draft. For read-only searches of large arrays, search [`current(draft)`](/docs/api-reference/current#searching-a-large-array) instead.

## Maps and Sets [#maps-and-sets]

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = {
  users: new Map([['ada', { name: 'Ada', age: 36 }]]),
  tags: new Set(['js']),
};

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => {
  // Update a value, and add and delete entries.
  draft.users.get('ada')!.age += 1;
  draft.users.set('grace', { name: 'Grace', age: 45 });
  draft.users.delete('ada');

  draft.tags.add('ts');
  draft.tags.delete('js');
});

expect([...state.users.keys()]).toEqual(['grace']);
expect([...state.tags]).toEqual(['ts']);
// The base state is unchanged.
expect(baseState.users.get('ada')!.age).toBe(36);
```

Values read from a Map or Set draft are drafts too, while Map keys are used as they are. See the FAQ for [iterating over Map drafts](/docs/extra-topics/faq#can-a-recipe-change-a-map-draft-while-iterating-over-it), [drafts as Map keys](/docs/extra-topics/faq#can-a-draft-be-a-map-key) and [the Set methods of ES2025](/docs/extra-topics/faq#do-the-set-methods-such-as-union-and-issubsetof-work-on-set-drafts).

## Returning a new state [#returning-a-new-state]

A recipe can return the next state instead of changing the draft, as a reducer does:

```ts
import { create, rawReturn } from 'mutative';

const baseState = { count: 5, history: [1, 2, 3] };

const state = create(baseState, (draft) => ({ ...draft, count: 0 }));

expect(state).toEqual({ count: 0, history: [1, 2, 3] });
expect(state.history).toBe(baseState.history);

// `rawReturn()` returns a value as it is, and can return undefined.
const cleared = create(baseState as typeof baseState | undefined, () =>
  rawReturn(undefined)
);

expect(cleared).toBe(undefined);
```

A recipe must either change the draft or return a new value; doing both throws. See [Returning a new state](/docs/api-reference/create#returning-a-new-state).

## Patches [#patches]

```ts
import { apply, create } from 'mutative';

const baseState = { todos: ['learn'] };

const [state, patches, inversePatches] = create(
  baseState,
  (draft) => {
    draft.todos.push('ship');
  },
  { enablePatches: true }
);

expect(patches).toEqual([{ op: 'add', path: ['todos', 1], value: 'ship' }]);
expect(apply(state, inversePatches)).toEqual(baseState);
```

See [Patches](/docs/advanced-guides/patches) for their format and for undo and redo.


# Introduction (/docs/intro)

Mutative is a JavaScript library for efficient immutable updates. Change a draft with ordinary JavaScript, and get the next immutable state.

**Mutative** is a JavaScript library for efficient immutable updates. A recipe changes a draft of the state with ordinary JavaScript, and Mutative produces the next state, copying only what the recipe changed. It was about 3.6x faster than Immer with matched settings and 6.6x faster with each library's defaults, across [97 benchmarked workloads](/docs/getting-started/performance).

## What is Mutative? [#what-is-mutative]

State that React, Redux and many other libraries compare by reference must not change in place: each update produces a new state, which copies the objects on the path to every change and shares all the others. Written by hand with spread syntax, such an update grows with the depth of the change, and a missed copy changes the previous state.

For example, take a state with a list, and mark its last item as done and add a new item, first by hand and then with Mutative:

```ts
import { create } from 'mutative';

const state = {
  list: [
    { text: 'Learn TypeScript', done: true },
    { text: 'Learn React', done: true },
    { text: 'Learn Redux', done: false },
  ],
};

// By hand, copying each level on the path to the changes:
const byHand = {
  ...state,
  list: [
    ...state.list.slice(0, 2),
    { ...state.list[2], done: true },
    { text: 'Learn Mutative', done: true },
  ],
};

// With Mutative, changing a draft:
const nextState = create(state, (draft) => {
  draft.list[2].done = true;
  draft.list.push({ text: 'Learn Mutative', done: true });
});

expect(nextState).toEqual(byHand);
// The unchanged items are shared, and the base state is unchanged.
expect(nextState.list[0]).toBe(state.list[0]);
expect(state.list[2].done).toBe(false);
```

The draft is a proxy of the state: Mutative copies an object the first time the recipe changes it, and the next state shares every object that the recipe left unchanged. See [Concepts](/docs/getting-started/concepts) for how it works.

## Features and Benefits [#features-and-benefits]

* **Mutation makes immutable updates** - Immutable updates of objects, arrays, Maps and Sets, written as mutations of a draft.
* **High performance** - About 6.6x faster than Immer with each library's defaults, and faster than hand-written spreads in measured wide-object and large-array insertion workloads.
* **Optional freezing state** - No freezing of immutable data by default, and [auto-freeze](/docs/advanced-guides/auto-freeze) when you want it.
* **Support for JSON Patch** - [Patches](/docs/advanced-guides/patches) use the `add`, `remove` and `replace` operations of JSON Patch, and with `pathAsArray: false` and `arrayLengthAssignment: false`, those of objects and arrays are JSON Patch operations.
* **Custom shallow copy** - [Marks](/docs/advanced-guides/mark) draft class instances and other types of immutable data, with their own shallow copies if needed.
* **Support mark for immutable and mutable data** - Marks set what is drafted without changing the data or its classes.
* **Safer mutable data access in strict mode** - [Strict mode](/docs/advanced-guides/strict-mode) makes reads of data that cannot be drafted explicit.
* **Support for reducer** - [Producers](/docs/advanced-guides/currying) work as reducers for Redux and any other immutable state library, and recipes can be async.

## Motivation [#motivation]

Immer made it easy to write immutable updates as mutations of a draft. Mutative keeps that model and focuses on performance: it copies each object at most once per update, drafts objects only when a recipe reads them, finalizes only the drafts that changed, and runs array methods that move elements natively on its copies. Immer freezes the next state by default, which costs time on every update; Mutative freezes it only when asked to.

Mutative also takes its options per call instead of from global configuration, drafts class instances through marks instead of changing their classes, supports async recipes and Map and Set subclasses, and handles [edge cases](https://github.com/unadlib/mutative/blob/main/test/immer-non-support.test.ts) that Immer gets wrong. [Comparison with Immer](/docs/extra-topics/comparison-with-immer) lists the differences.

## Credits [#credits]

Mutative is inspired by [Immer](https://immerjs.github.io/immer/), which has helped many people write simpler immutable updates. Mutative is based on the same idea, with a different implementation and more features.
